newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace swimmers hold oil rig in stranglehold.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace swimmers hold oil rig in stranglehold.

text.p: Greenpeace protesters continued to swim in front of a British Petroleum oil rig to stop it reaching an oilfield on Friday, the sixth day of a cat and mouse game in the north Atlantic.
Activists had been in the water most of the night to keep the Stena Dee platform from reaching the new Foinaven field, which is about 100 miles north of Scotland, Greenpeace said.
The lobby group is also blocking a rig off the Alaskan coast to keep it away from a field in the arctic Beaufort Sea.
The blockades, aimed to fight global warming, are part of Greenpeace's most ambitious campaign against the oil industry.
Both sides have had their fair share of high-profile battles, with the lobby group more than once emerging as David beating Goliath.
But so far the clashes have been over well-defined ground -- the most notable being Greenpeace's successful opposition to Shell's plans to sink the Brent Spar oil buoy in open sea.

This time round Greenpeace wants to strike at the very heart of a $550 billion-a-year industry, and the campaign is not just directed at development of Foinaven or the Prudhoe Bay field off Alaska's north coast.
The lobby group wants an end to all fossil fuel exploration across the globe and urges the oil industry to focus instead on alternative energy sources.
Greenpeace, which is convinced fossil fuels are causing climate change, predicts "rapid and unpredictable ecosystem damage" if oil and gas production continues to increase.
But there is still good money to be found in oil and $150 billion a year is spent to find more black gold.
The sheer magnitude of these investments makes the outcome of the current battle almost predictable.
The platforms will be delayed, but that cannot prevent Prudhoe Bay or the Atlantic frontier from becoming major oil provinces.
With wind and solar power very expensive, "the oil companies should be left to get on with their valuable work in the deep ocean," the Financial Times said.
But through its campaign, Greenpeace will undoubtedly succeed in winning more support for renewable energy.
Even BP has said it would support the development of solar energy to help cut carbon dioxide emissions.

"We must now focus on what can and what should be done, not because we can be certain climate change is happening, but because the possibility can't be ignored," BP's chief executive John Browne said in a ground-breaking speech in May.
Browne also said BP saw solar power as a profitable investment, aiming for one billion dollars in sales over the next decade.
Wind power, according to the Washington-based Worldwatch Institute, is already the fastest growing energy source, growing by 26 percent last year.
But in all, renewable energy still only satisfies one to two percent of total world energy needs.
Meanwhile, carbon dioxide emissions rose three percent last year to 6.25 billion tonnes, a Worldwatch Institute report found.
Change might come. A proposed treaty to curb emissions will be discussed in Japan in December by 152 countries after five years of negotiations.
But already the motor industry has warned the treaty could seriously hurt economies in developed countries.
"It's about the sharing of wealth and jobs for the next 30 years," said Ford chairman and chief executive officer Alex Trotman.
Greenpeace predicts floods, poor crop yields and disease if drastic action is not taken now, and is calling for a 20 percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions from 1990 levels by the year 2005.
"We don't have the luxury of time for green rhetoric or blinkered politics," said Greenpeace spokeswoman Mirella Lindenfels here.
"The precautionary principle says act now."
